summary: Ustaz Azlan tells two episodes from the Prophet's SAW life between the ages of 14 and the early twenties, before he met Khadijah: the Fijar War, which grew out of a dispute over a trading tender and ended in a killing in a sacred month, and the Hilf al-Fudul pact, which committed its parties to defend the wronged. From the war the Prophet SAW was trained in resilience and in putting peace first; from the pact came a commitment to justice that he held for the rest of his life.
keyPoints: The Fijar War began with a dispute over a trading tender that ended in a killing in a sacred month, and the tribal gang mentality dragged whole tribes into the fight.
Seeing war shaped the Prophet's SAW resilience and his habit of putting peace first whenever conflict broke out.
The war lasted around four to five years before it was settled by negotiation and the payment of blood money.
Hilf al-Fudul was a pact to always defend the wronged, whoever the wrongdoer was, even one's own tribe.
The Prophet SAW said he would rather have taken part in that pact than own red camels, and that he would answer such a call again even after Islam.
A Muslim must not take a 'none of my business' attitude toward injustice, and may work with anyone on the principle of justice as long as nothing contradicts the shariah.

chapters.title: Introduction: character training from childhood
chapters.summary: The ustaz recalls the elements that shaped the Prophet's SAW character from childhood and introduces the two episodes before Khadijah.

chapters.title: The Fijar War and the meaning of its name
chapters.summary: The war took place when the Prophet SAW was 14 or 15 according to Ibn Hisham, and is called the sinful war.

chapters.title: Nu'man's tender and the killing of Urwah
chapters.summary: A dispute between Al-Barrat and Urwah over a tender to carry goods to the Ukaz market ended in murder.

chapters.title: Tribal mentality and the sacred months
chapters.summary: A small quarrel drew in whole tribes, and the killing took place in a sacred month and violated the sacred land.

chapters.title: The Prophet's SAW role in the war
chapters.summary: The war lasted four to five years; scholars differ on how far the Prophet SAW took part.

chapters.title: Lessons from growing up in war
chapters.summary: Children who live through war build resilience, and the Prophet SAW learned to put peace first.

chapters.title: The effects of conflict and the danger of extremist recruitment
chapters.summary: The ustaz links the effects of conflict to young people recruited by extremist groups and to trauma at home.

chapters.title: The end of the war and the start of Hilf al-Fudul
chapters.summary: The war was settled by negotiation and blood money, then came the event that led to the pact when the Prophet SAW was around 20.

chapters.title: The Yemeni trader and Al-As ibn Wa'il
chapters.summary: A Yemeni trader was cheated by Al-As ibn Wa'il and made his complaint in verse on Mount Abu Qubays.

chapters.title: Zubayr and the sealing of the pact
chapters.summary: Zubayr ibn Abdul Muttalib gathered several tribes at the house of Abdullah ibn Jud'an to defend the wronged.

chapters.title: The meaning of Fudul and 'none of my business'
chapters.summary: The name of the pact is linked to goodness, and the ustaz stresses the duty to oppose injustice at least in the heart.

chapters.title: The Prophet's SAW words on the pact and the lesson of justice
chapters.summary: The Prophet SAW said he preferred the pact to red camels; the ustaz explains the Muslim's wide social engagement across causes.

lessons.title: Tribal mentality is jahiliyyah
lessons.body: Backing 'our side' without weighing right and wrong is a jahili trait that returns today on social media.

lessons.title: Respect the sacred months and the sacred land
lessons.body: The four sacred months, Rajab, Dhul Qa'dah, Dhul Hijjah and Muharram, were agreed as a time without fighting.

lessons.title: Resilience is built by hardship
lessons.body: Children living in war zones build extraordinary resilience, and the Prophet SAW was trained in a similar setting.

lessons.title: Put peace first in conflict
lessons.body: The Prophet SAW disliked pouring oil on a fire and always looked for the point where peace could be made.

lessons.title: Learn history from those who lived it
lessons.body: Do not provoke with past events you do not understand; listen to the people who lived through them.

lessons.title: Care for young people's mental health
lessons.body: Young people recruited by extremist groups often have psychological problems and lack affection, not only religious conviction.

lessons.title: Domestic violence leaves its mark on children
lessons.body: A child who sees a father hit a mother may repeat it unknowingly, even after resolving not to.

lessons.title: Trading during Hajj is permitted
lessons.body: The Hajj season is also a chance to trade and meet people from many countries, in line with the spirit of the Quran.

lessons.title: Defend the weak without favouritism
lessons.body: Defending the wronged even when the wrongdoer is from one's own tribe was the principle of Hilf al-Fudul.

lessons.title: 'None of my business' is not the attitude of a believer
lessons.body: Hating injustice at least in the heart is the weakest level of faith; feeling nothing at all means no faith.

lessons.title: Justice is an Islamic principle
lessons.body: A Muslim can work with anyone as long as it rests on justice and does not contradict the shariah.

lessons.title: Activism is not limited to causes with a religious label
lessons.body: Defending animals and protecting the environment, including recycling at mosques, also falls under justice.

glossary.meaning: The war called 'sinful' because it was fought in violation of the sacred months and sacred land.
Wickedness or sinfulness, the root of the name Al-Fijar.
Four months in which fighting and bloodshed are forbidden: Muharram, Rajab, Dhul Qa'dah and Dhul Hijjah.
The sacred territory of Makkah, which must not be stained by bloodshed.
Tribal partisanship, backing one's own group regardless of right or wrong.
Blood money, compensation for a life or an injury.
The pact to defend the wronged, sealed at the house of Abdullah ibn Jud'an.
Goodness; the ustaz also mentions the view that it carried the sense of 'none of your business' in the mouths of those who rejected the pact.
A rare and very costly camel, a byword for valuable wealth.

dalil.context: The ustaz mentions that Allah SWT permits trading during Hajj. (reference identified, verse number not stated)
dalil.translation: but it is no offence to seek some bounty from your Lord. When you surge down from Arafat remember God at the sacred place. Remember Him: He has guided you. Before that you were astray.

dalil.context: Used to argue that a 'none of my business' attitude toward injustice is not allowed.
dalil.translation: Whoever sees a wrong should change it with his hand; if he cannot, then with his tongue; if he cannot, then with his heart, and that is the weakest of faith.

dalil.context: The Prophet SAW recalls Hilf al-Fudul and states the value of that pact.
dalil.translation: I witnessed a pact at the house of Abdullah ibn Jud'an; I would rather have taken part in it than own red camels, and if I were invited to it again in Islam, I would go.
